title: B2 · L22 — Phrasal verbs: conflicts
topic: Phrasal verbs for arguments and conflicts
description: Phrasal verbs de conflictos: fall out, make up, patch up, put down, stand up to.

questions.prompt: Un amigo te cuenta que ya no habla con su hermano por una herencia.
questions.question: What does 'to fall out with someone' mean?
options: To fall in love with someone.
To have a serious argument and stop being friends.
questions.explanation: 'Fall out with' significa pelearse seriamente y romper la relación — sugiere una ruptura duradera, no una discusión pasajera. Muy usado en familias, amistades y contexto laboral. Cuidado: no confundir con 'fall in love' (enamorarse) — misma preposición inicial, significados opuestos.
examples: They fell out over money years ago and haven't spoken since. → conflicto familiar
I fell out with my best friend last year — we're finally starting to reconnect now.

questions.prompt: Dos amigas se reconcilian tras una gran pelea.
questions.question: Complete: 'After weeks of arguing, they finally ___ ___ and are friends again.'
questions.explanation: 'Make up' (with someone) significa reconciliarse después de una pelea. Es el antónimo directo de 'fall out'. Muy común en relaciones familiares, amistades y parejas. Nota: 'make up' tiene múltiples significados (inventar, aplicar maquillaje, compensar) — el contexto lo aclara.
examples: We had a huge fight but somehow made up within a few hours. → relación de pareja
It's time to make up and move on — life's too short for grudges.

questions.explanation: FALSO — significa exactamente lo CONTRARIO. 'Put someone down' es menospreciar, hacer sentir mal, humillar con palabras. Es una forma común de acoso verbal o crítica destructiva. En contextos de salud mental y RRHH se identifica como conducta tóxica. También existe 'put yourself down' (auto-menosprecio).
examples: Stop putting your brother down all the time — it's really damaging his confidence. → intervención familiar
He constantly puts his colleagues down in meetings. Nobody wants to work with him.

questions.text: It's important to stand up to bullies rather than let them push you around.
questions.explanation: 'Stand up to' significa enfrentarse a, plantar cara a alguien poderoso o abusivo. 'Push someone around' significa dominar, tratar mal. Vocabulario típico de discursos anti-bullying, RRHH y psicología. Prosodia: énfasis en 'stand up' y 'push you around'. Connected speech: 'push you' se enlaza 'pʊʃ-ju'.
examples: He stood up to his boss for the first time last week — genuinely proud of him. → hito laboral
You need to stand up to her — she can't keep treating you like that, it's not on.

questions.prompt: Un matrimonio pasa por terapia para salvar la relación.
questions.question: What does 'to patch things up' mean?
options: To repair a damaged relationship after a conflict.
To keep quiet about a problem.
questions.explanation: 'Patch up' significa reparar (una relación, un problema, una herida). Sugiere una solución parcial o pragmática, más suave y menos definitiva que 'make up'. La metáfora viene de coser un parche sobre una tela rota — arregla, pero se ve la costura. Muy usado en contextos donde la reconciliación no es total pero es funcional.
examples: They somehow managed to patch up their marriage after the affair. → segunda oportunidad
Let's try to patch things up before it gets any worse — we can't afford to lose him.

questions.statement: 'To pick on someone' significa criticarles o acosarles repetidamente.
questions.explanation: VERDADERO. 'Pick on' significa meterse con alguien de forma repetida e injusta, elegirle como blanco constante de bromas, críticas o bullying. Muy usado en contextos escolares (bullying infantil) y laborales (mobbing). Un clásico del vocabulario de acoso: 'stop picking on me', 'why are you always picking on him?'.
examples: The other kids picked on him mercilessly because of his glasses. → recuerdo escolar
Why are you always picking on me? Just leave me alone for once.

questions.prompt: Empareja cada phrasal verb de conflicto con su continuación natural:

pairs.left: We need to patch things up
You must stand up to him
pairs.right: if you want to be respected.

questions.explanation: Familia semántica de verbos de conflicto: fall out (romper relación), patch up (reparar parcialmente), put down (humillar verbalmente), stand up to (enfrentarse), make up (reconciliarse). Todos son B2+ y esenciales para narrar tensiones interpersonales con precisión.
examples: They fell out and stopped speaking for over a decade. Real tragedy. → historia familiar
It's high time to patch things up. This silent treatment has gone on long enough.

questions.prompt: Un sindicato cede ante la presión empresarial en una negociación.
questions.question: What does 'to back down' mean?
options: To retreat from a position or argument.
questions.explanation: 'Back down' significa retirarse, ceder, abandonar una postura defensiva. Común en negociaciones, confrontaciones políticas, disputas legales. Es similar a 'give in' (rendirse) pero enfatiza más el retirar la propia posición que el aceptar la ajena. Usarlo bien te posiciona con vocabulario de análisis geopolítico y de negocios.
examples: He refused to back down from his position, even when the pressure became intense.
The union backed down after the CEO's final offer — a controversial move at the time.

questions.target: I don't want to fall out with my sister over something so trivial, but she keeps pushing my buttons.
questions.explanation: Combinación 'fall out with' + 'push my buttons' (provocarme). Prosodia: tono frustrado pero contenido, énfasis en 'trivial' y 'buttons'. Nativos añaden 'honestly' o 'to be fair' para mostrar autoconciencia y no sonar demasiado acusatorios. Confesión típica de conflicto familiar.
examples: I fell out with him over the silliest little argument — I still don't know how it escalated.
She really knows how to push my buttons. Twenty years and I still fall for it. → observación fraternal

questions.prompt: Un colega se queja del comportamiento tóxico de un jefe.
questions.question: Complete: 'Please stop ___ ___ my ideas in every meeting.'
questions.explanation: 'Shoot down' (an idea/proposal/suggestion) significa rechazar tajantemente sin considerar seriamente. Muy usado en reuniones profesionales para describir el rechazo destructivo. La imagen viene de derribar un avión — cae y ya no vuela. Es un signo de mala gestión cuando se hace sistemáticamente.
examples: He shot down every single suggestion I made in the strategy session. → queja laboral
Don't shoot down her idea before at least hearing her out properly. That's not how we work.

questions.statement: 'To smooth things over' significa reducir la tensión tras un conflicto.
questions.explanation: VERDADERO. 'Smooth over' significa suavizar, calmar tensiones, quitar aristas de una situación conflictiva. Es una forma diplomática de gestionar problemas, aunque a veces sin resolverlos completamente. Común en contextos corporativos y familiares donde la armonía superficial importa. Metafóricamente: alisar una superficie rugosa.
examples: She tried her best to smooth things over between them, but the damage was already done.
Let's smooth this over before the client notices anything is wrong. → gestión de crisis

questions.text: After the argument, they didn't speak for weeks, but eventually they patched things up.
questions.explanation: Historia clásica de conflicto y reconciliación gradual. 'Patch things up' aquí sugiere que la relación se reparó, aunque quizás no completamente. Prosodia: pausa reflexiva tras 'weeks', tono más cálido al final. Connected speech: 'patched things up' fluye con la /d/ suave. 'Eventually' recibe énfasis temporal.
examples: We patched things up after a long talk over coffee — worth every uncomfortable minute.
It took time and effort, but we patched it up. Not perfect, but functional.

questions.prompt: Una manifestante mantiene su posición pese a la presión.
questions.question: Complete: 'She refused to ___ ___ despite intense pressure from her colleagues.'
questions.explanation: 'Give in' significa ceder, rendirse ante la presión ajena. Similar a 'back down' pero enfatiza más el momento de rendirse ante la insistencia externa que el abandono de una postura activa. También se dice 'give in to temptation/pressure/demands'.
examples: Don't give in to their unreasonable demands — hold your ground. → consejo negociador
She finally gave in after hours of exhausting arguing. Simply too tired to keep fighting.

questions.target: I really need to stand up to my manager. He keeps taking credit for my ideas and I've had enough.
questions.explanation: Situación laboral universalmente relatable. 'Take credit for' es colocación fija (atribuirse el mérito). Prosodia: tono decidido pero controlado, énfasis emocional en 'had enough'. Nativos suavizan añadiendo 'you know' o 'honestly' para mostrar la deliberación detrás de la decisión.
examples: It's genuinely time to stand up to him. This has been going on for too long. → confesión con mentor
I've had absolutely enough of his behaviour. Something needs to change, and soon.

questions.prompt: Un informe interno investiga fallos de gestión.
questions.question: Which phrasal verb means 'to accuse someone of doing something'?
questions.explanation: 'Point the finger at' es una metáfora vívida (señalar con el dedo) que significa acusar públicamente a alguien de ser el culpable. Muy usado en periodismo, informes de investigación, disputas legales y conflictos laborales. Es más dramático y explícito que 'blame' — implica señalamiento público visible.
examples: The independent report pointed the finger at senior management for the failures. → crónica corporativa
Don't point the finger at me — I wasn't even in the office that week!
